newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities remain stagnant.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities remain stagnant.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options remained stagnant in slow late afternoon trading as underlying bond prices barely moved, dealers said.

While time-decay worries continued to pressure option premiums, implied volatilities were already at historically very low levels and were also underpinned by caution ahead of Tuesday's March consumer price index (CPI), they noted.
"In the big picture, it's still very low," said a trader for a brokerage firm. "So if you're expecting a good move out of CPI, it might not be a bad idea to get long (options)."
"But after that (CPI) comes out, I would imagine it (volatility) is going to come off even more," he added.
Traders said the battered bond market could take another hit from CPI, given Friday's losses on stronger than expected March producer prices.

Economists polled by Reuters have forecast, on average, a rise of 0.2 percent for the overall March CPI against a gain of 0.3 in February, and a 0.3 percent March rise for the core rate excluding food and energy against February's 0.2 percent.
Implied volatility for June T-bond futures options stood at around 8.9 percent, virtually unchanged from Friday.
Traders said there were very few sizable deals in the pit today.

One house was said to have bought 3,000 contracts of May 108 calls, delta-neutral against futures -- apparently a high-gamma volatility play. May options expire shortly on Friday and therefore have high gamma, which gives them quick price acceleration against swings in underlying futures.
A second house was seen buying 2,500 June 108 calls.
The 108 calls were slightly out of the money, with June futures drifting narrowly around Friday's 106-20/32 close.
Volatilities were mostly steady across the board at the shorter end of the yield curve as well.
Implied volatilities for June, September and December Eurodollar futures options on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange stood at around 7.1, 10.2 and 11.9 percent respectively.

"There's very little going on," a brokerage trader at CME said. He noted that the two biggest trades today were spreads in mid-curve options, which are options that expire in coming months but are priced off futures expiring in 1998.
One house was said to have traded 2,000 lots of a short-June 92.50/92.75/93.00 "Christmas tree" spread.
The firm bought the 93.00 puts and sold the 92.50 and 92.75 puts.
Another firm was seen doing a short-May 92.50/92.75/93.00 put butterfly, buying the outside strikes and selling the middle.
The "red June" (June 1998) futures, which the short-May and short June options settle against, were off three basis points at 93.04.
Shin Kishima/Chicago Derivatives Desk ((312-408-8750))
